I'm done with the search, so here's the answer.

**Verdict:** The vault has no churn benchmark from Hormozi, so I can't give you a number he endorses. What it does have is what he did when members of his own paid community, Skool Games, were cancelling: he found out why they left and cut things. The main reason was overwhelm, not missing value, so he took things away.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). It rests on one close example: his own paid community and the cancellations it had.

**How we get there**
1. His own community's churn: "the number one reason that people were cancelling was overwhelm. It was not oh I need to provide more value. It was I need to provide more value per second in fewer total seconds" ([yt--JLN1d1ZKUU @ 11:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=662s)). His fix was to cut three weekly calls to one and move the big content download from monthly to quarterly. He also turned off app features so new members had "fewer things to do when they got in", because otherwise they think "I can't think about it. And then they leave" (@ 11:35).
2. The rules behind it, from his thinking page: **simplify by subtraction**, meaning "you only introduce something when it's required or necessary for that person to get the the desired value" (@ 11:35). And **if not enough people say yes, make the offer better**: "if we can't get enough people to say yes we need to make the offer better" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:24:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5089s)).
3. Applied to your question: in the vault he never treats churn as a number to compare against an industry average. He treats it as a sign that the product isn't working for members, and fixes the product. So "when should I worry?" becomes: worry when you don't know why people cancel.

**What he'd most likely tell you to do**
- **Find the number one reason people cancel.** Ask them. He'd want one specific answer, not a vague one. He believes fear "only exists in the vague not in the specific" ([yt-XGm2ERU9qtA @ 20:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=1246s)).
- **Check the first days for overwhelm.** Too many calls, a content dump or too many features means people leave before they get any value. Give them one valuable first step, then show the next one.
- **Watch for the urge to add more.** His point was that his members didn't need more value. They needed more "value per second" in less of their time.
- **Speed up the first result.** "latency beats magnitude 7 days a week" ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 15:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=953s)). The sooner members get a win, the more likely they are to stay.

**Not in the vault (from his wider work, not quoted):** in his gym and community content, Hormozi often uses a "hypothetical max": new members per month divided by monthly churn gives the size where the community stops growing. For example, 50 new members a month at 10% churn caps out at about 500 members. He also treats lifetime value as roughly price divided by churn. Use this to decide whether churn is a problem: if the cap is below your goal, cutting churn is the biggest lever you have. Typical churn for paid communities is often quoted at roughly 5 to 10% a month, but that's general industry talk. None of the sources in this vault say it, and it isn't a Hormozi quote.

**What would change his answer:** if people were cancelling because they got the result and were done, not because they were overwhelmed. Then cutting things wouldn't help. The money-models side would matter more, like offering the next thing at the right time. The vault covers that idea only in general terms ([[business/offers/money-models]]).

**Caveat:** this vault has only 6 sources, and none of them is about churn. A vault built from his Skool and community content would probably have his actual numbers.

**Verdict:** Hormozi would take the percentage of revenue, and specifically a percentage of the *extra* revenue your work brings in. The vault never shows him comparing profit and revenue directly. But his own example of how a consultant should get paid is a cut of the uplift they create, and his rule about capped downside and uncapped upside also points to revenue.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). He describes a percentage-of-uplift deal himself, but he never directly compares it with profit share.

**How we get there**
1. **The closest thing he said** (Diary of a CEO, 2023): "I'm able to increase your conversion onite by 20% Okay cool so now that's doing $1.2 million a year I made $200,000 in value and maybe I can get 10% of that I get 20 grand" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:38:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=2283s)). In his example the consultant gets 10% of the revenue increase. Profit doesn't come into it.
2. **The rule behind it:** "when you have a a capp downside, an uncapped upside, that is the recipe for opportunity" ([yt-XGm2ERU9qtA @ 15:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=909s)).
3. **Applying it to your choice:** Revenue goes up or down with your work. Profit also depends on things you don't control, like the client's payroll, ad spend, rent and accounting choices. A client can grow revenue 20% because of you and still report no profit, and then 20% of zero is zero. That's a downside someone else sets for you. This step is my reasoning from his rule, not something he said.

**Why he'd say it**
- **What you're really selling.** He says buyers "don't really want your time. They want to buy an outcome." ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 14:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=852s)). The outcome you can show is more revenue. Their cost structure isn't your outcome.
- **Keep the deal simple.** He says "fancy equals friction simple equals sales" ([yt-JDR-R--4HhM @ 32:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=1927s)). Revenue is a single number from the payment processor, which is easy to check. Profit share leads to arguments over what counts as a cost.
- **The client matters more than the split.** His larger point in that passage is that the same work for a bigger business pays far more: "I make them $20 million for my 20% bump and I get 10% that and I make $2 million 20,000 2 million 100x same work" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:38:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=2318s)). He'd ask how big this client's revenue base is before he'd care much about the profit-or-revenue question.

**What he's done:** Acquisition.com takes equity, which pays out of profit and value, usually as 25 to 49% stakes. He accepts that because it acts as a growth partner with influence over the whole business ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 33:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=2038s)).

**What would change his answer:** Profit share (or equity) makes sense if you're effectively an operator who has a say in costs as well as sales. That's the Acquisition.com model. If you're an outside consultant working on one lever, take revenue, and ideally measure it against a revenue baseline you both agree on before you start.

**Verdict:** Bootstrap, and let your customers fund it. Charge a high price to a few buyers, collect the cash up front, and put it back into growth. On this model, outside money comes later, once the business already works.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). The vault has no source where Hormozi talks about raising money versus bootstrapping. That's after searching for "investor", "raise", "bootstrap", "venture", "capital", "debt" and "equity" in both the wiki and the raw transcripts. The verdict comes from his stated rules on how to fund an early business.

**How we get there**
1. **The nearest case he did address is how to fund growth when you're starting.** His answer is to sell your own time at a premium and reinvest the cash. He says to "be willing to take 5 10% of your time, charge 10 times more and make enough income from that that you can take all the other money and go aggressive" ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 15:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=919s)). He did this himself: one cash-paying personal-training client covered his living costs, so all the gym's money could go into growth ([@ 1:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=97s)).
2. **The rule behind it is to pull cash forward through your money model.** He describes a money model as "how do you pull cash forward accelerate cash conversion uh within a business so that you can scale" ([yt-tGhe3sBuk34 @ 8:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=497s)). In his view, growth capital comes from how you charge, not from someone else's cheque.
3. **The new case falls under that rule.** A first business usually has no proof yet. His starting playbook is to sell something expensive to a few people ("it is significantly easier when you're starting to sell extremely expensive to a select few", [yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 0:32](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=32s)). That gives you cash and market feedback before you'd need investors.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Margin and learning.** "If you trade your time for the money, you have a 100% margin" ([@ 6:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=360s)). He also calls it "a great way to beta test ideas" ([@ 4:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=297s)).
- **The market is the judge.** "If we can't get enough people to say yes we need to make the offer better" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:24:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5089s)). On this logic, if customers won't pay, the fix is the offer, not funding.
- **Capped downside.** "When you have a a capp downside, an uncapped upside, that is the recipe for opportunity" ([yt-XGm2ERU9qtA @ 15:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=909s)). He also says "fear comes from having something to lose" ([@ 14:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=876s)). Taking investor money or debt into an unproven business adds obligations, which works against that.

**What he's done:** He built Gym Launch from about $1,000 left in December 2016, with no investors mentioned. It reached $26M top line in its first 12 months by licensing his gym system for cash ([profile](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=1714s)). He now invests through Acquisition.com, which usually takes 25–49% stakes as a growth partner in companies that already exist ([@ 33:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=2038s)). So he is an investor himself, but in businesses that already work, not in first-timers' ideas.

**What would change his answer:** If you're already making money and your money model breaks even or better on acquiring customers, he says the goal becomes "to spend as much money as humanly possible uh while maintaining break even or better" ([yt-tGhe3sBuk34 @ 8:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=497s)). At that point, capital from a partner could speed things up. Capital is one of the four kinds of leverage he lists, along with labor, media and technology. The inference also weakens if your business can't sell anything until heavy upfront R&D is done, like deep tech or hardware. The vault doesn't cover that case.

**Caveats:**
- The vault contains only six sources, five of them his own 2025 videos.
- The "sell your time" advice comes from a video that also promotes his funnel.
- **Beyond the vault (not in the vault):** He is widely known for publicly preferring customer-funded, profitable businesses over venture funding. No quotes on this are captured here, so don't treat it as cited.

**Verdict:** Hormozi wouldn't give you a time-blocked calendar. He'd tell you to pick the one thing that would most change your revenue in the next 12 months, which for an under-earning business almost always means getting more customers or a better offer. Then spend most of your day doing a set daily quota of that work, and let everything else wait. Nothing in the vault shows him prescribing a daily schedule, so the "how" below is worked out from his rules.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). The rules are among his best-supported, but he never addressed the case of a "new full-time founder's workday."

**How we get there**
1. **Name the one thing.** "what one thing if it were true 12 months from now would change everything for our business" ([yt--JLN1d1ZKUU](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=232s) @ 3:52). If you can't name it, he says you're "not doing my job and I need to think about it longer" (@ 12:08).
2. **"Not enough money" is a verdict on your offer and your volume.** "if we can't get enough people to say yes we need to make the offer better" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5089s) @ 1:24:49). And "10 out of 10 times, the person limiting the business, limiting your growth is you" ([yt-XGm2ERU9qtA](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=941s) @ 15:41).
3. **So the day should be built around inputs, not tasks.** "if you do not know the inputs that are going to get the output that you want then what are you doing" (yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 38:58).

**What that looks like as a day**
- **Most of your hours go to the one thing**, usually selling and getting leads. Set a daily number (calls, outreach messages, consults, offers sent) that's "so much volume that it is unreasonable that you fail" (yt-XGm2ERU9qtA @ 9:04). He measures sales skill in rejections: "I have to collect 5,000 NOS" (yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 47:48).
- **Everything else comes after the quota.** "sometimes you have to let the little fires burn" (yt--JLN1d1ZKUU @ 6:04). Admin, tweaking the website and new side projects all wait. He says the price of compounding is "the length of time you have to say no to everything else" (yt-XGm2ERU9qtA @ 22:58).
- **If cash is tight, sell a small slice of your time at a premium.** "be willing to take 5 10% of your time, charge 10 times more and make enough income from that that you can take all the other money and go aggressive" ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=919s) @ 15:19). Cap it: "just cap it."
- **Cut out learning that doesn't change what you do.** "if you watch more videos, but your conditions are the same and your behavior does not change, you entertained yourself" (yt-XGm2ERU9qtA @ 5:39).
- **Hours:** if you're under 30 with no responsibilities, "working as many hours per week as humanly possible because you will never be able to work this hard again" (yt-XGm2ERU9qtA @ 11:52). His own rule for when to stop: "I work until I can't work meaning like my put per unit of time starts to drop precipitously" (yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:09:28).

**What he's done:** At his first gym he taught every class and still ran his own sales consults at 8, 9, 10 and 11 p.m. for about six months (yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 55:05).

**What would change his answer:**
- **If customers already say yes but you can't take on more**, the one thing is delivery or hiring, not sales.
- **If you have kids or other responsibilities**, he no longer pushes maximum hours. He says you have trade-offs but more experience to spend effort strategically.
- **If you love your life as it is**, he says "you've already won." In 2023 he refused to tell anyone how much they *should* work ("there is no should").

Caveat: five of the vault's six sources are videos on his own channel, which also promote his books and Acquisition.com.

**Verdict:** Keep the cash for growth and pay the debt on schedule, as long as the business covers the payments easily. Hormozi's push to get out of the hole is about people who can't pay their bills. A profitable business with payments it can cover isn't in that position. His rule for spare cash is to put all of it into growth, "go on the offense with it."

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: low to medium). The vault has no source where he talks about business debt, so this applies his rules to your case.

**How we get there**
1. The closest thing he said is "get yourself out of the hole as fast as humanly possible" ([[yt-XGm2ERU9qtA]] @ 17:53, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=1073s). The context is personal survival: "I get that you can't have a vision if you have bills to pay, if rent is due." The fix he gives is "Work three jobs… Just get your head above water. At that point, options open up." Being in the hole means you can't cover your obligations. It doesn't mean having any debt at all.
2. Once you're above water, his rule is to use the money for growth. In his bootstrap advice, you cover your living costs with a small, capped income stream, "and then cash flow all the growth… take all the other money and go aggressive, go on the offense with it" ([[yt-uWdIgftpvBI]] @ 15:19, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=919s). He did this himself: one cash-paying training client covered his own needs, so he "could reinvest all of the gym's money into growth" ([[yt-uWdIgftpvBI]] @ 1:37).
3. You're profitable, so you're above water. That puts you under rule 2. Paying the $60k early would mean spending growth money on a problem that isn't stopping you from growing.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Leverage.** "understanding how to get more for what you put in is the game overall" ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:44:08). Cash that earns more in the business than the interest you'd save should stay in the business.
- **One thing at a time.** Ask "what one thing if it were true 12 months from now would change everything for our business" ([[yt--JLN1d1ZKUU]] @ 3:52). Paying off a manageable loan is rarely that one thing. Usually it's one of the "little fires" he says you can let burn.
- **Capped downside, uncapped upside.** "when you have a a capp downside, an uncapped upside, that is the recipe for opportunity" ([[yt-XGm2ERU9qtA]] @ 15:09). Debt you can service has a fixed, known cost, while growth spending has no ceiling. That's the trade he favors.

**What he's done:** He paid for his early gym's growth out of its own cash flow and kept his personal income separate ([[yt-uWdIgftpvBI]] @ 1:37). He also lost everything once: a partner emptied the bank account, a payment processor froze six months of funds, and by December 2016 he had $1,000 left ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 18:34). He knows what happens when cash disappears.

**What would change his answer**
- **The debt really is a hole.** If the payments squeeze cash flow, the rate is punishing, or one bad month would mean you can't pay, the "oxygen mask" advice applies and you clear it first.
- **The debt is driving your decisions.** He says "fear comes from having something to lose" ([[yt-XGm2ERU9qtA]] @ 14:36). If worry about the $60k makes you play it safe, it's costing you more than the interest.
- **You have no specific growth use for the cash.** He sends you back to inputs: "if you do not know the inputs that are going to get the output that you want then what are you doing" ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 38:58). If you can't say what the money will do, paying down debt beats letting it sit.

My own note, not his: compare the after-tax interest rate with the return you're actually getting on growth spending, and keep a few months of operating costs in reserve either way.

The vault's thinking page shortens the 17:53 quote to "Get out of debt fast," which overstates it. In the transcript he talks about rent and bills, not business debt. I haven't changed the vault. I can correct that line, or save this answer to `derived/`, if you want.

**Verdict:** There's no calendar refresh in anything he's said, so don't schedule one. Keep running your best ad (the "control") until something beats it, and use the ad budget to test new hooks against it all the time. If refreshing copy and hooks still doesn't bring results back, he'd say the offer is the problem, not ad fatigue.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: **low–medium**). The vault never mentions ad fatigue, refresh frequency or creative rotation. I searched "ad fatigue", "creative refresh", "facebook ads", "new ads", "control", "split test" and "stop working" in both the wiki and the raw transcripts. What follows applies his nearest stated rules.

**How we get there**
1. **The hook decides whether the ad works, and you judge it against a control.** "a banger or killer headline can absolutely outperform the control by two three sometimes 5x" ([yt-JDR-R--4HhM @ 0:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=36s)). He talks about beating a control, not about a set lifespan for an ad. That suggests a rule like "replace it when a challenger wins or the numbers drop" rather than "replace it every N days."
2. **Good advertisers never stop working on hooks.** "the best advertisers the more they've been doing it the more they obsess on the hook they obsess on the headline because they know that's where the money's at" ([@ 1:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=73s)). Testing hooks is ongoing work, not a quarterly task.
3. **Where new hooks come from:** "look at your organic content or other people's organic content or other people's ads look at the first 3 seconds visually and verbally" ([@ 1:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=111s)). You can also borrow from other industries: "can I steal like an artist from a different industry" ([@ 2:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=146s)). His own organic posts that do well become your ad hooks.
4. **Volume over polish** (from his thinking page): "then you just have to do so much volume that it is unreasonable that you fail" ([yt-XGm2ERU9qtA @ 9:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=544s)). Applied to ads, you'd always have several new hooks in test, not one carefully made replacement every month.
5. **If responses keep falling, look at the offer first:** "if we can't get enough people to say yes we need to make the offer better" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:24:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5089s)). He also calls the offer "the highest leverage thing I think you can do in the business" ([@ 1:25:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5123s)).

**In practice, his way**
- Let the numbers tell you when to refresh. When click-through or cost per lead on the control gets worse, swap in a new hook. The calendar doesn't decide.
- Write each test variant with a deliberate headline. "never run an ad without a headline" (@ 1:13). He'd test the hook first, because that's where he says most of the gain is.
- Keep the body copy and the PS line the same while you test hooks, so you know which change caused the result.

**What would change his answer:** if your audience is small and the same people see your ads many times (high frequency), the hook stops working faster just from repetition. Then you'd need new hooks more often, but the trigger is still the numbers dropping, not a set date. Also, Hormozi has talked about ad volume and creative testing in *$100M Leads* and elsewhere, but none of that is in this vault, so I haven't cited it. Adding those sources would make this answer stronger.

**Verdict:** Hormozi would tell you to raise your prices. He would not hold them flat to protect the close rate. When 82% of the people you inspect say yes, you have more demand than your price reflects, and his rule is that demand like that should push your price up. He would also have you add a premium tier at roughly 10x your main ticket. You're optimizing the wrong number: close rate matters less than profit per inspection.

**Based on:** this follows from what he's said (confidence: high). He never talks about duct cleaning or names a close-rate threshold in this vault. But his "when you have demand, raise the price" rule shows up in two sources, and it applies directly to your situation.

**How we get there**
1. **What he said about the nearest case.** Asked about a craftsman with more demand than he can serve, he said "you have demand because you're so good at it you can either raise the price and just continue to keep raising the prices until eventually become Versace of of of wallets and you make tons of profit" ([Diary of a CEO, 2023 @ 1:29:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5386s)). In 2025 he put it more bluntly: "when you have demand, cut supply." Limited supply "forces you to raise your price," but only "as long as you don't have limiting beliefs" ([If I Started A Business in 2026 @ 5:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=328s)).
2. **The rule behind it.** From his thinking page: sell to the people who value you most, charge more, and start high and work down, never staying stuck in the middle.
3. **Why your case fits.** An 82% close rate on in-home inspections means almost no one who sees your price turns it down. He would read that as proof you have demand. Keeping prices flat to protect it is the "limiting belief" he describes. He also tells you to "destroy should," including the idea that a close rate should stay high.

**Why he'd say it**
- **You're in the middle.** "either sell extremely expensive stuff to a select few or sell something super cheap to everyone. The middle is where people die." ([@ 0:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=0s))
- **Add a tier around 10x your main ticket and state the price out loud.** "you simply make a 10 times more expensive offer, you will have a percentage likelihood that is greater than zero that someone will buy it." ([@ 18:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=1086s)) And: "If they want to pay you more money, you should give them the opportunity to do so." ([@ 7:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=425s)) He says the high tier also makes the core package look more valuable. In the home, "You must confront the high price," then "We shut up. We let them talk." ([@ 8:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=489s), [@ 8:41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=521s))
- **Build the premium tier around speed and ease, not a longer list of services.** "take whatever the delivery time you currently have is and cut it in half." "You will always have priority. You will always be first in line." ([@ 16:25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=985s)) For you, that could mean same-week scheduling, a whole-home package with before-and-after camera footage, an annual plan, and handling everything so the homeowner does nothing.
- **Look for the customers who value you most.** "solve rich people problems they pay better" and "find the people who value what you have the most" ([Diary of a CEO @ 1:38:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5918s)). In one company he invested in, 15% of customers bought the top package. The business was rebuilt around that group alone, and prices went up 10x.
- **Use the market's answer to adjust.** "if we can't get enough people to say yes we need to make the offer better" ([@ 1:24:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5089s)). If the close rate falls too far, the fix is a better offer, not a lower price.

**The numbers (my arithmetic, not his):** Suppose you raise prices 20% and your cost per job stays the same. Profit per job goes from 38% to about 58% of today's ticket. To earn the same total profit, you'd only need about two-thirds as many jobs, which is roughly a 54% close rate. Anything above 54% means more profit, and your crews have more open time. You can test this cheaply on a slice of inspections, and if it fails you just roll it back. That's the kind of bet he likes: the downside is capped and the upside isn't.

**Beyond the vault:** Outside these sources, Hormozi often says that closing most of the people you pitch means you're underpriced. That line isn't in this vault, so I haven't quoted it, but it says the same thing as the reasoning above.

**What would change his answer:** if the 82% only holds because inspections are pre-sold by a cheap lead offer or an insurance or warranty channel, so price isn't really being tested. It would also change if you can't take more work and lack the capacity for a premium tier, though his "cut supply" logic still says raise the price in that case. The real exception is a low-cost model built on volume ("super cheap to everyone"). At a 38% margin with in-home sales, you aren't running that model.

My own view: he would likely skip one practical risk. Residential customers compare quotes, so raise prices in steps and watch close rate by lead source, rather than jumping 10x on your core service.
